A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CoTFormer and retain its central mechanism of attending to intermediate token representations. The text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison. v1 has no appendices; v2's Appendices A-C are present and readable.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-modeling experiments on OpenWebText2 and PG19, including three-run perplexity results in Table 1 and Figure 2.

after.justification: v2 reports original OpenWebText2 experiments, adaptive-computation evaluations, architecture ablations and comparisons of halting methods, including results in Appendices B-C.

M1.justification: v2 retains basic CoTFormer but adds LN-CoTFormer with non-repeated beginning/end layers and normalization after repeats. Sections 4.1-4.2 introduce Mixture of Repeats: learned routing, capacity-based token selection, interpolated updates, randomized training capacities and depth embeddings. Token-adaptive inference was only future work in v1.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates language modeling on both PG19 books and OpenWebText2. v2 retains only OpenWebText2, with no PG19 evaluation preserved in its appendices. Removing the entire book-domain benchmark substantially narrows dataset and domain coverage.

E2.justification: Standard and Block Universal Transformers remain comparators. v2 adds an adaptive LN-Block Universal comparator in Figure 4 and directly compares Stick Breaking and PonderNet halting against Mixture of Repeats in Appendix C, Table 4. This substantially extends the evaluated comparisons into adaptive computation.

E3.justification: The retained OpenWebText2 experiments change from 20k training steps with 400 warmup steps to 40k with 8000 warmup steps, alongside a redesigned layer/repeat sweep. v2 adds 60k-step adaptive training, 10k-step halting comparisons, operation-count evaluation and inference-budget sweeps using calibrated router capacities. These are substantial protocol changes.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's depth/repeat comparisons, v2 adds reserved-layer and normalization ablations (Table 2), depth-embedding ablations for fixed and adaptive repeats (Appendix B), router versus fixed-depth analysis (Figure 4), and training-duration effects on router distributions (Figure 5). Figures 2-3 also investigate accuracy-compute trade-offs and sequence-length-dependent computation costs.

E5.justification: Table 1 in both versions reports means of three runs with standard errors. However, v1 Figure 2 displays error bars, whereas the replacement performance plots in v2 Figure 2 omit them. This changes graphical uncertainty reporting while retaining the main table's aggregation practice.

E6.justification: The original results are extensively replaced, and PG19 entries disappear. v1 reports 24x2 CoTFormer versus 48-layer standard perplexities of 28.69 versus 28.89; under v2's longer training, these are 25.28 versus 24.17. The new LN-CoTFormer with five middle-block repeats reaches 24.11 (Table 2). Adaptive-budget, ablation and halting-comparison results are also added. Cross-version scores do not establish same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 adds mathematical definitions of routing scores, capacity-based selection and interpolated updates for variable repeats. This is a limited extension of the formal method definitions. Equations (1)-(3) largely reformulate the retained architecture; neither version supplies original theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v1 centers on obtaining deeper-model performance through intermediate-token attention. v2 makes adjustable inference computation a central contribution and claims improved accuracy-compute trade-offs and stable adaptive training. Its abstract and conclusion also qualify larger-model matching through architectural tweaks, extending the paper's main contribution beyond fixed-repeat parameter efficiency.

C2.justification: v1 briefly acknowledges attention overhead and leaves adaptivity unresolved. v2 adds substantive explanations of computation bottlenecks, routing and capacity sampling, plus limitations involving normalization-related loss spikes, poorer performance at minimum compute budgets and insufficient training of deeper repeats. Section 5 also acknowledges needing more repeats than the nominal depth ratio to match deeper standard models.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the Pre-LayerNorm backbone, batch size 128, Nvidia A100 80GB hardware and use of non-causal FlashAttention with adapted masking. It adds relative training-time information, PonderNet's selected penalty weight and code-access instructions in Appendix A. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the code link's availability was not externally verified.

R1.justification: The brief parameter-sharing and CoT discussion becomes substantially broader positioning against ACT/PonderNet, Mixture-of-Depths, Sparse Universal Transformer, theoretical CoT studies and explicit-reasoning approaches. v2 distinguishes its weight sharing and prefix repeats from Mixture-of-Depths and argues complementarity with explicit reasoning training and Pause Tokens.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title, substantially rewrites the abstract and introduction, and replaces the sequence-interleaving exposition with a token/context recurrence presentation. Related work moves before the method, experiments are organized around fixed and adaptive computation, and the discussion gains structured subsections. This is extensive narrative reorganization beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is retained, but v1's three-panel performance bar chart becomes two accuracy-compute plots. Table 1 changes from dataset columns and effective-depth groups to repeat-count columns grouped by base depth. v2 adds computation-cost, adaptive-budget and router-distribution figures, plus three ablation/comparison tables, substantially revising the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrates parameter savings but leaves compute efficiency and adaptive depth largely untested. v2 addresses these central gaps with quantified accuracy-compute trade-offs, adaptive inference, component ablations and explicit failure conditions, supported by substantially better implementation documentation. Removing PG19 narrows generality, and Appendix C's short halting comparisons provide limited evidence. Nevertheless, the new analyses and qualifications substantially strengthen the paper's support for its practical contribution.
